# mm

mm is a box for what you are not doing yet. Your head is for the work. The box holds the rest.

A gap with nothing in front of you turns into a scroll or the next episode. Put the next piece of work in the queue before that gap. When it opens, `mm` already has the next thing.

An idea during study or deep work has nowhere to sit. `mm add "write this up later"` lines it up behind the work you are in. You stay on that work. When you finish, the idea is next. A tiny nag uses `mm add -q` and stays off the line.

If something more important comes up, `mm add -p` puts it on the stack. Finish it with `mm done` and you are back.

Nothing appears unless you type `mm add`. Tomorrow the item is gone unless you add it again. There is no config file, no daily seed, no habits, and no calendar.

## Two times it helps

- A gap in the work. The empty minute is when a feed or another episode takes the hour, because they start without a decision. Put the next real thing in the queue first. When the gap opens, `mm` already has it.
- An idea during deep work or study. Add it with `mm add`. It waits behind the work you are in. You stay on that work. When you finish, the idea is next. A tiny nag can go to quick with `mm add -q` so it does not join the line.

## The three places

- queue — the line of real work. `mm add "task"`. First added, first done.
- stack — something just became more important. `mm add -p "task"`. Last stacked, first done. Then the queue is where you were.
- quick — a small nag. `mm add -q "task"`. It does not jump the line. Clear it with `mm flush-quick`.

Bare `mm` is `mm next`.

## Against other workflows

- In your head: you rehearse the list instead of doing the work. Working memory holds about four chunks (Cowan, 2001).
- A todo list: it stores tasks, then asks you to choose again.
- A calendar: it decides when. mm never does.
- Getting Things Done: same first move (get it out of your head), then projects, contexts, and a weekly review. mm stops at the three places.
- Notes, tabs, and paper piles hold tasks. They do not name the interruption or put you back.

## Why this shape

- Cognitive offloading (Risko & Gilbert, 2016): write the task down so attention can stay on the work.
- Attention residue (Leroy, 2009): leaving a task unfinished leaves attention behind. The stack plus `mm done` is the way back.
- Interruptions (Mark): returning to the original task takes on the order of 23 minutes. The queue is the written return address.
- The Zeigarnik effect (remembering unfinished tasks better) has not held up as a general rule. mm does not rely on it.

## Install

macOS and Linux:

```
git clone https://github.com/Toseef-Ahmad/mm.git
cd mm && ./install.sh
```

Windows (Command Prompt or PowerShell, three lines):

```
git clone https://github.com/Toseef-Ahmad/mm.git
cd mm
install.cmd
```

Python 3.11+. No pip dependencies. State is one file: `~/.mm/state.json` (`%USERPROFILE%\.mm\state.json` on Windows).
